meta.question: How do production agents detect that they are stuck in a loop, and what do they do about it?
meta.title: Loop detection
meta.hook: Gemini CLI asks a second model if the agent is looping. OpenHands matches patterns. LangGraph just counts steps.

answer: There is no single technique. Gemini CLI runs three detectors at once: hashed tool-call cycles, repeated text, and a periodic model-based check that a second model must confirm. OpenHands matches five patterns over the recent event history. Both warn the model once before stopping it. LangGraph has no behavioural detection, only a step budget, and no loop detector was found in Codex.

repos.summary: A dedicated `LoopDetectionService` with three independent detectors, a one-time recovery message, and a hard stop on the second detection.

repos.what: The agent SDK and server behind OpenHands (the OpenHands/OpenHands repository is now the UI)
repos.summary: A `StuckDetector` that compares recent actions and observations against five stuck patterns, nudges the model on repeated errors, and otherwise marks the conversation `STUCK`.
The runtime does not look at behaviour. It counts steps and raises `GraphRecursionError` at the limit; recognising an unproductive loop is left to the graph you write.
No loop detector or step cap was found in the core turn loop at this commit. A turn continues until the model stops asking for follow-up work or the user cancels.

deep_dives.headline: Three detectors, one warning, then a stop
how_it_works: Every stream event passes through `LoopDetectionService.addAndCheck`. For tool calls it hashes the tool name plus its JSON arguments with SHA-256 and appends the hash to a short history. It then looks for a repeating cycle: any pattern of length 1 to 5 that has repeated 5 times in a row. That catches `A A A A A` and also `A B A B A B A B A B`.

For model text, it slides over the stream in 50-character chunks, hashes each one, and flags a loop when the same chunk appears 10 times within a short distance. Tracking is switched off inside code blocks, where repetition is normal.

Neither catches an agent that keeps doing slightly different unproductive things. So once a single prompt has run for 30 turns, the service periodically sends the last 20 turns to a model with a diagnostic prompt and asks for a confidence score. At 0.9 or above, a second model alias has to agree before a loop is declared. The interval between checks adapts between 5 and 15 turns: the more suspicious the last result, the sooner the next check.

The response is graduated. On the first detection `GeminiClient` clears the flag, injects a system-style message telling the model a loop was detected, and continues. On the second detection it emits `LoopDetected` and ends the turn.

deep_dives.headline: Five named patterns over the last few events
how_it_works: `StuckDetector.is_stuck` looks only at events since the last user message, so a new instruction resets the picture. It collects the most recent actions and observations and tests five scenarios in order.

The scenarios are: the same action producing the same observation 4 times; the same action producing an error more than 3 times; the agent sending 3 messages in a row with no action; a two-step alternating pattern over 6 events; and a loop of context-window errors.

Repeated errors get special treatment. When an action has failed with the same error exactly 3 times, `get_action_error_nudge` returns a message naming the tool and the error, which the conversation injects as a user-role message. The nudge fires once per streak. If the streak continues past the threshold, the conversation is marked stuck.

When a pattern matches, the run loop sets the execution status to `STUCK` and stops. Thresholds are a small config object that callers can override, and detection can be turned off when creating the conversation.

deep_dives.headline: A step counter, and the rest is up to you
how_it_works: LangGraph runs a graph in steps. When a run starts, the loop computes a stop point: the current step plus `recursion_limit`. On each tick it checks whether the step has passed that point and, if so, sets its status to `out_of_steps`.
The caller then raises `GraphRecursionError`, with a message suggesting a higher limit. The default limit is read from an environment variable and is 10007 at this commit.

The prebuilt ReAct agent adds one courtesy on top. It tracks remaining steps in its state, and if the model asks for more tool calls with fewer than 2 steps left, it replaces the response with a short message saying it needs more steps, so the run ends cleanly without an exception.
Nothing here inspects what the agent is doing. If you want to notice the same tool being called repeatedly, you add that as a node or a check in your own graph.

deep_dives.headline: No detector found: the loop trusts the model and compaction
how_it_works: Codex's core turn function runs a plain `loop`. Each pass sends a sampling request; if the model asked for tool calls, they are executed and the loop goes round again. It exits when the model returns only a message and nothing else is pending, or when the turn is cancelled.

No code was found in `codex-rs/core` that compares successive tool calls, counts repeats or caps the number of passes. The one place the code mentions an infinite loop is a comment about context growth: as long as compaction brings the context back under the token limit, the loop is not expected to run away.
So the safeguards at this layer are the model's own judgment, automatic compaction when the token limit is reached, and the user interrupting.

differences.title: Exact match versus judgment
differences.detail: Gemini CLI and OpenHands both start with exact matching, which is cheap and has few false positives. Only Gemini CLI adds a model as judge for loops that exact matching cannot see, and it pays for that with extra model calls.

differences.title: Call only, or call plus result
differences.detail: Gemini CLI hashes the tool call alone. OpenHands requires the observation to match too, so polling a command whose output changes is not treated as a loop.

differences.title: Both warn before they stop
differences.detail: Gemini CLI injects a warning on the first detection and stops on the second. OpenHands nudges on repeated errors and stops on the other patterns. Neither kills the run at the first sign.

differences.title: Products detect, the framework budgets
differences.detail: The two products that implement detection own the whole loop, so they can watch it. LangGraph does not know what your nodes mean, so it offers a step budget and leaves behaviour to you.

differences.title: How long before a hard cap
differences.detail: The step caps differ by two orders of magnitude: 100 turns per prompt in Gemini CLI, 500 iterations per run in OpenHands, 10007 steps by default in LangGraph.

build_your_own: Start with a step cap. It is one line, and it is the only protection LangGraph gives you by default.
Add exact-match detection on tool calls: hash the name and arguments, keep a short history, and look for cycles, not only identical consecutive calls. Gemini CLI's version is under 40 lines.
Compare results as well as calls if your agent legitimately polls. OpenHands' action-plus-observation rule avoids that false positive.
Warn the model once before stopping it. Both implementations do, and a message naming the tool and the error gives the model something to act on.
Give 'stuck' its own status, separate from error and finished, so callers and UIs can respond differently.
Only add a model-based check if exact matching is missing real loops, and gate it the way Gemini CLI does: after many turns, at a high confidence threshold, confirmed by a second model.
